title: Stage 67, Lesson 8: Reading git diff - what the AI changed, and in which file
subtitle: A comparison of two versions shows every change, including the ones the AI's report doesn't mention.
whyItMatters: In the lesson on boundaries, you told the AI to change only one thing and then asked it to list its changes. But that list is still the AI telling its own story. Git diff is different: it is a comparison generated by the machine between two versions, showing every added and removed line in every file. Once you can read it, you have evidence instead of a promise, and it takes only a few minutes.
openingQuestion: You told the AI to change only the Send button, and it says it is done. What is the fastest way to find out which files it really changed?
openingOptions: Look at the git diff, the comparison of the old and new versions
Ask the AI 'did you change anything else?' and trust it
Open every file and read it from top to bottom to find anything unusual
Test the page to see whether the Send button now works, which is enough
explanation: Git diff lists exactly which files changed and which lines were added or removed, compared by the machine rather than told by the AI. Asking the AI again still relies on its word, and it may forget extra edits it made. Opening every file takes very long and doesn't show what is new. And testing only shows that the Send button works, not whether other files were changed.

diagram.label: Ask for the diff: a comparison of two versions of the project
Question 2: is any file outside the scope you gave?
Question 3: are the removed lines worrying? Then accept, or ask to restore

realWorldExample.description: Illustrative scenario: someone tells an AI to fix only the Send button. The AI's report mentions only the Send button. Opening the diff, they see that a pricing file was also changed and fifteen lines were removed. With three questions and two minutes of reading, they ask for that pricing file to be restored and keep the button fix. Without the diff, the pricing mistake would have shown up when a customer placed an order.

quiz.question: In a git diff, what does a line starting with - mean?
options: A line with an error that needs to be fixed in the next round
A comment line that the machine skips when running the program
A line newly added in the new version of the file
A line that was in the old version and was removed from the new one
quiz.explanation: The - sign marks a line from the old version that is no longer in the new one. A newly added line starts with +. The - sign has nothing to do with comments or with whether the line has an error; it only says this line has been dropped.

quiz.question: What does the line '+++ b/gia-tien.js' in a diff tell you?
options: The name of the file that the changes below belong to
The file gia-tien.js has already passed three rounds of testing
The file gia-tien.js has been deleted from the project entirely
Three new lines have just been added to the file gia-tien.js
quiz.explanation: This header line simply names the file that the changes below it belong to. The three plus signs are header notation, not a count of added lines. It says nothing about testing, and a deleted file is shown in a different way.

quiz.question: What are the three questions for reading a git diff quickly?
options: Who wrote it, when, and in which language
Which files changed, is any outside the scope, are the removed lines worrying
How many words, how many lines and how many characters there are
Whether the code is pretty, whether it is short, and whether it has many comments
quiz.explanation: These three questions hold to your goal: keep changes within scope and lose nothing that was working. Who wrote it or when does little to decide whether to accept. Counting words and characters says nothing about content. Pretty or short code is not the right yardstick for accepting work.

quiz.question: You only asked for a fix in nut-gui.js, but the diff also changes gia-tien.js. What should you do?
options: Delete both files and ask the AI to start over from the beginning to be sure
Accept it as is, because the extra file may be a better improvement
Ask why that file changed, and restore it if it isn't needed
Ignore it, because it is enough that the Send button works
quiz.explanation: A file outside the scope is exactly what the previous lesson told you to block. Asking the reason and then deciding to keep or restore it is how you stay in control. Accepting it or ignoring it lets an unreviewed change slip in. Deleting both files would throw away the button fix that was correct.

quiz.question: Why should you look at the diff before accepting the AI's fix?
options: The diff proves the new code works without needing to run it again
The diff helps the AI remember the scope you gave it in the last turn
The diff makes the program run faster by dropping the extra lines
The diff shows exactly what changed, including what the report missed
quiz.explanation: The machine generates the diff from two real versions, so it leaves nothing out, including what the AI forgot to mention. It does not replace testing, because it tells you what changed but not whether it is right. The diff also sends nothing to the AI, and it does not make the program faster.

keyTakeaways: Git diff is a comparison of two versions generated by the machine, not a story told by the AI.
A + line is added, a - line is removed, and '+++ b/file-name' shows which file is changing.
Three questions: which files changed, is any outside the scope, are the removed lines worrying?
For a file outside the scope you gave, ask why, and ask to restore it if it isn't needed.
The diff shows what changed; you still have to test to know whether the change is right.

practicePrompt.question: You only asked for a fix to the Buy button. The diff has 2 added lines in nut-mua.js and 15 removed lines in tinh-gia.js. What is the most worrying thing?
options: tinh-gia.js, outside the scope, lost 15 lines; ask why
Only 2 added lines is too few to fix a button
The file name nut-mua.js uses a hyphen, so the machine may not understand it
The diff is longer than one page, so the fix is probably wrong
practicePrompt.explanation: The risk is that lines were removed from a file you never asked it to touch, and that file does the pricing. A small number of added lines does not signal a problem: fixing a button sometimes takes only two lines. Hyphens in file names are normal. The length of a diff doesn't tell right from wrong; what matters is which files it touches.

summary.keyIdea: Git diff gives you evidence of every change, so accepting or restoring has a basis.
summary.formula: Diff = changed files + added lines (+) + removed lines (-); read it with three questions before accepting.
summary.commonMistake: Trusting only the list of changes the AI tells you, without looking at the diff the machine generated.
summary.action: Next time you ask an AI to make a fix, ask for the diff and read the list of files before opening any file.

application.title: Do it now in 10 minutes
application.message: Ask an AI to fix one small thing in a project that has version control, with a sentence setting the scope. Then ask to see the git diff and answer three questions: which files changed, is any outside the scope, are any removed lines worrying?
application.secondary: If you don't have a diff tool yet, ask the AI to show you the two versions side by side, file by file.

sections.text: In the last lesson you set a boundary and asked the AI to list its changes. But that list is still written by the AI, and it may forget. Git diff is a comparison generated by the machine, so it is more trustworthy. This lesson teaches you to read it: you only need to recognise a few symbols and ask three questions.

sections.title: Git diff is simpler than you think
sections.intro: Picture handing a contract to someone else to edit. To see what they changed, you switch on comparison mode: deleted words are struck through, new words are highlighted. Git diff does exactly that for code.
rows: A line that is in the new version and not in the old one
A line that was in the old version and is no longer in the new one
The name of the page being edited
The file that has changes below this header
The page and line number of the edit
The position in the file where the changed section starts
sections.oneLiner: A diff is a comparison: + lines are added, - lines are removed, and the header says which file.

sections.caption: A small diff. The header shows the file, the @@ line shows the position, the - line is removed, and the + lines are added.

sections.title: Three questions for reading a diff quickly

steps.label: Which files changed?
steps.detail: Read the '+++ b/...' lines first: they are the list of files with changes.

steps.label: Is any file outside the scope?
steps.detail: Compare the list with what you told the AI; mark any unfamiliar file.

steps.label: Are the removed lines worrying?
steps.detail: Look at the lines starting with -: removed rules, checks or pricing are where you should stop.

steps.label: Decide
steps.detail: Accept, ask for the reason, or ask to restore a specific file.

sections.text: Why look at the diff before accepting

The AI's report is a story, while the diff is evidence. Testing tells you the Send button now works, but not whether the AI changed the pricing file. The diff answers exactly that question, and reading it with three questions takes only a few minutes, even for someone who has never written code.

left.label: Accept on the strength of the report
left.text: The AI says it fixed the Send button, you see the button work and accept. The pricing file was changed quietly, and the mistake only shows when a customer places an order.

right.label: Look at the diff, then accept
right.text: The list of files shows the pricing file changed and lost fifteen lines. You ask why, ask for it to be restored, and keep only the button fix.

sections.label: Connecting to the last lesson
sections.text: The boundary you set in the last lesson is the yardstick. The diff is what you measure with it: any file outside the boundary, stop and ask.

sections.title: The diff has an unfamiliar file

s1.text: You told the AI to change only nut-gui.js. It says it is done. You ask for the diff and see two files: nut-gui.js and gia-tien.js, and gia-tien.js has lost three lines.

choices.label: Ask why gia-tien.js changed, look at the removed lines, and ask to restore it if it isn't needed
The Send button works, so accept; the other file is probably a small change

bad_accept.text: The three removed lines were the code that rounds prices. A few days later customers report odd prices, and you have to hunt for what the AI removed.

good.text: The AI says it removed the rounding line to make things tidier. You ask to restore the pricing file and keep the button fix. The final version differs only where you asked.

sections.label: Running project: the Alley coffee shop - step 8/10
sections.text: Step 8: finish the function phanTich so that it counts added lines and removed lines, lists the files that changed, and catches any file outside the scope you gave.

sections.title: Project step 8: read a git diff and catch changes outside the scope
sections.task: You told the AI to change only nut-gui.js. It returns a git diff: a line starting with + is added, a line starting with - is removed, and "+++ b/file-name" shows which file is changing. The function phanTich currently only counts lines and doesn't know file names: it counts both header lines "+++" and "---" as real changes, and it doesn't report any file outside the scope. Fix the function so it prints the correct number of added lines, the number of removed lines, the list of changed files, and the files outside the scope.
sections.expectedOutput:
Added 4 lines, removed 2 lines
Changed files: gia-tien.js, nut-gui.js
Outside the scope: gia-tien.js
hints: Run it first: added 6, removed 4 is wrong, because the two "+++" lines and the two "---" lines are wrongly counted as changed lines.
Check for lines starting with "+++" or "---" BEFORE you check for "+" or "-".

lines: The diff is evidence: see which files changed, which are outside the scope, and which removed lines are worrying.
